content: In 2018, the Canadian toxicovigilance network, known as Covigilance Canada, was expanded to reflect its growing membership, which exceeded 350 members by 2019. This network fosters interdisciplinary and jurisdictional collaboration among poison centers, public health agencies, health security organizations, regulatory bodies, non-governmental organizations, and academic partners. It also includes experts from clinical toxicology, forensic laboratories, public safety, law enforcement, border services, and their international counterparts. Although the components of Toxicovigilance Canada are at various stages of development, there has been a notable increase in information exchange, trust, and collaboration aimed at preventing poisonings, improving treatment, and reducing harm. The organization emphasizes a comprehensive approach to risk assessment and management of toxic exposure events of public health concern. It provides a trusted environment for the following activities: Timely detection, validation, and notification of signals and trends related to toxic exposure events of public health concern, as reported by Canadian poison centers through the Surveillance System. Detection of toxic substances through laboratory analysis, data-sharing, and information exchange on analytical methods, as well as mutual aid among clinical toxicology and forensic laboratories via the Toxicology Laboratory Response Network. Notification and alerting through an early warning system, supported by expertise within the Toxicovigilance Canada network. Access to a geographically searchable Canadian Antidote Registry to support clinical treatment, antidote planning, and stockpiling. Enhanced public awareness of safety signals and guidance through collaboration within the Public Outreach and Communications Working Group. In the European Union, several rapid alert systems exist for different product categories. One such system is the Rapid Alert System for Chemical Incidents, managed by the European Commission. This system facilitates information-sharing among EU poison centers and national public health authorities regarding unusual poisoning cases, mass intoxications, and chemical incidents. It employs standardized terminology for clinical effects to identify similar cases and analyzes system records daily. Information exchange across organizations and countries improves early detection of trends and potential cross-border incidents. Events that may pose serious cross-border health threats, as defined under Decision 1082/2013/EU, are reported to the Early Warning Response System by designated national focal points, similar to the process for public health emergencies of international concern under the International Health Regulations (2005). The Scientific Committee on Health, Environmental, and Emerging Risks can rapidly assess risks associated with newly identified health and environmental exposures to consumer safety or public health, as requested by the European Commission. These assessments may include serious or cross-border health threats involving chemical events. Another rapid alert system, Safety Gate, addresses dangerous non-food consumer products, excluding food, pharmaceuticals, and medical devices, which have their own alert systems. Safety Gate enables rapid information exchange among national authorities in 31 countries and the European Commission regarding hazardous products on the market, including chemical hazards and risks such as choking hazards in children's products. The Rapid Alert System for Food and Feed, established in 1979, allows efficient information-sharing among food and feed authorities in member states to coordinate rapid responses to health threats, such as contaminated food or feed products. This system can lead to product recalls from the market. In France, since January 1, 2016, the Agence nationale de sécurité sanitaire de l'alimentation, de l'environnement et du travail (ANSES) has coordinated the national toxicovigilance scheme and the toxicovigilance activities of French poison centers. These centers provide 24-hour poison information services to the public and health professionals and conduct toxicovigilance in collaboration with regional health agencies. They document detailed information on poisoning cases, including patient details, exposure context, substances involved, clinical toxicity observed, treatments provided, and medical outcomes. Periodic studies are conducted on substances of interest, such as dimethyl fumarate. In the United Kingdom, the National Poisons Information Service (NPIS) has conducted pesticide surveillance since April 2004, monitoring cases requiring healthcare consultations. Data on exposures are collected through access to the NPIS online clinical toxicology database TOXBASE and telephone inquiries to its four units (Birmingham, Cardiff, Edinburgh, and Newcastle). Currently, 1,563 TOXBASE entries for pesticides and biocides are tracked. These data demonstrate the utility of poison centers in monitoring pesticide exposures, leading to improved healthcare. A broader surveillance program with TOXBASE flags 142 chemicals of special interest, including 26 highly toxic substances used in chemical warfare or previously released deliberately. NPIS units receive automatic email alerts when TOXBASE users access information on these chemicals, serving as an early warning for potential environmental, industrial, or terrorist events. Since 2006, all national clinical data have been logged in the United Kingdom Poisons Information Database, accessible to all NPIS units for surveillance and toxicovigilance to identify patterns or trends in inquiries. In the United States, a network of 55 poison centers provides 24-hour information and advice to the public and health professionals. Each center documents inquiries in a standardized format to collect demographic, exposure, health management, and outcome data for each case. These data are uploaded in near real-time to the National Poison Data System (NPDS), maintained by the American Association of Poison Control Centers. The NPDS contains data on over 66 million calls since 2001. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) uses this database to enhance public health surveillance for chemical, radiological, and biological exposures and illnesses, identify early markers of such events, and increase situational awareness during suspected or known incidents. The NPDS conducts three algorithm-based automated surveillance activities: monitoring hourly call volumes compared to historical reference values, tracking the number of reported incidents of 131 clinical features, and case-based surveillance for exposure to 11 case definitions associated with substances of interest. When anomalies are detected, medical toxicologists and epidemiologists review the cases to assess public health risks. If an incident of public health significance is identified, alerts are sent to local and government public health departments to ensure a prompt response. In 2010, the CDC and the American Association of Poison Control Centers established a poison center public health community of practice to enhance collaboration among federal, state, and local health agencies and poison centers. This community, now with over 250 members, has been instrumental in fostering a multidisciplinary approach to public health surveillance.
